newsitem.title: UK: EMS VIEW - French budget worries nipped in the bud.
newsitem.headline: EMS VIEW - French budget worries nipped in the bud.

text.p: After weeks in which the 1997 French budget was painted as a death knell for monetary union, a series of well-orchestrated leaks from Paris has left foreign exchange players wondering what exactly the fuss was all about.
With nine days to go before the presentation of the budget plans to parliament, analysts acknowledge there are few details left to find out that will have potential to roil the markets.

The French government, through a series of accounting sidesteps and ambitious assumptions, has again managed to make its numbers add up. Importantly, the budget looks likely to avoid agitating French labour unrest to a higher pitch.
The plans leaked so far allow France to publicly retain its commitment to Maastricht budget deficit criteria and keep the goal of monetary union in 1999 on track, analysts said.

"The franc has rallied since the budget plans were leaked last week and it's not really clear what people were expecting to be so shocking from this budsget in the first place," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.
At 1000 GMT today, the French franc was trading at 3.4148/53 per mark up more than one-and-a-half centimes from a five-month low at 3.4315 set last Thrusday.

Von Maydell said that UBS do not think the French will manage the three-percent target ratio for budget deficit to GDP next year because of overzealous forecasts on growth and the 1996 deficit, but this fact was never likely to be fresh news to the market.
With the Maastricht criteria almost certain to be interpreted in the relaxed way the Treaty wording allows for, the remainder of the EMU process will be chiefly a political issue.
If anything, analysts argue, the inventive French accounting shown over the past week makes the whole budgetary process more credible than many people assumed even this time last month.

"We now know almost every element of the budget and there's very little next week that will be a major surprise," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch. "Overall, what we've seen looks pretty reasonable and nothing like the disaster that many people were painting recently."
Prendergast said he now expects the franc to settle in a range between 3.4050 and 3.4300 per mark for the near term.

For many traders, the details are more complicated than the limited exchange rate volatility justifies. Despite the jitters, the mark/French franc rate has risen a maximum of just one percent since the beginning of August.
"I think a lot of people jumped the bandwagon on this whole story and at the end of the day no one is quite sure what they're looking for," said one trader at a Swiss bank in London.
Based on an economic growth forecast for 1997 of 2.3 percent, the French government is aiming for a total public deficit of 3.O percent of GDP next year.

Key to this is the commitment to freeze central government spending at 1996's targetted 1,552 billion francs. Allowing for inflation and prior commitments, this means an additional 60 billion francs of spending cuts have to be made next year.
This will be achieved by cutting between 6,500 and 7,000 civil service jobs, savings of 15 to 20 billion francs in job subsidy cuts and a reduction in housing aid subsidies.
These cuts are the key bones of contention for French labour unions. But, analysts said that these issues were fought over last year and there is nothing here that adds to labour's ire.
Many of the leading French union chiefs have already puiblicly stated that the protests and strikes planned for the next couple of months will not be on the scale of 1995.

Pension reform lifts the revenue side, meantime. A 37.5 billion contribution from French Telecom will be written into state accounts at 1997 income as the state assumes longer-term pension liabilities during Telecom's partial privatisations.

To sweeten the whole package, tax cuts of 75 billion francs over five years were announced late last week. Although the new net tax cut is a more prudent 18 billion, however, analysts said the tax cuts will have a positive psychologicial effect.
